items.title: DSM categories don't always carve nature at the joints
items.claim: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual is the standard US classification of mental disorders. What's the standard critique?

options.text: DSM categories perfectly match underlying biology

Categories were chosen by committee consensus; high comorbidity between disorders, dimensional features within categories, and biological heterogeneity all suggest DSM may not reflect natural kinds. The NIH RDoC (Research Domain Criteria, 2010) proposes a dimensional alternative for research
DSM has only one category for all disorders

items.reveal:
DSM-5 (2013) maintained categorical diagnosis under pressure to introduce dimensional aspects. Thomas Insel (then NIMH director) announced in 2013 that NIMH would 're-orient' research away from DSM categories toward RDoC.

Key problems: ~60% of patients meet criteria for two or more disorders simultaneously; treatment response often crosses diagnostic boundaries; genetic studies (Cross-Disorder Group, 2013) show overlapping risk variants across disorders.

ICD-11 (WHO, 2022) introduced some dimensional elements.
items.why: Diagnostic categories shape research, insurance and stigma. The categories matter clinically even where their scientific basis is questioned.

items.title: Bowlby's monotropy claim has been substantially revised
items.claim: John Bowlby's original theory emphasised a single primary attachment figure (typically the mother). What does subsequent evidence suggest?

options.text: Monotropy is fully supported by all evidence

Infants form attachment hierarchies with multiple caregivers (Schaffer & Emerson 1964); fathers, grandparents and consistent non-parental carers can serve as attachment figures; quality matters more than exclusivity
Only mothers can be attachment figures

items.reveal:
Schaffer and Emerson's 1964 Glasgow study followed 60 babies and found by 18 months most had multiple attachments; nearly a third had primary attachment to someone other than the mother. Lamb's (2010) reviews of father involvement showed independent contributions to child outcomes.

The monotropy claim, alongside Bowlby's earlier ideas about 'maternal deprivation', shaped 1950s-60s policy (working mothers, daycare, hospital visiting). Rutter's 'Maternal Deprivation Reassessed' (1972) sharpened the distinction between privation (no attachment formed) and deprivation (loss of formed attachment).
items.why: Theories with policy implications need re-examination as evidence accumulates. Bowlby's core insight (attachment relationships matter) survives; the specific claim of monotropy has been substantially revised.

items.title: Placebo effects are real but smaller than often claimed
items.claim: Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche's 2010 Cochrane meta-analysis of 234 trials of placebo versus no treatment found:

options.text: Placebos rivalled active drugs for most conditions
Placebos had small effects on continuous subjective outcomes (especially pain and nausea); little effect on objective outcomes; placebo effect in everyday discourse exaggerates the clinical evidence
Placebos had no measurable effect at all

items.reveal:
Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche's Cochrane review pooled randomised trials comparing placebo with no treatment. Effects on objective outcomes (blood pressure, tumour size) were near zero; effects on subjective ones (pain ratings, anxiety) were measurable but modest.

Open-label placebos (Kaptchuk et al. 2010) — patients told they're receiving placebo — still produce effects for some conditions, suggesting expectation and clinical ritual play roles beyond deception.
items.why: Placebos matter for clinical trial design (controls), patient communication and understanding what 'treatment effect' means — but the popular framing oversells what placebos can do.
